paragraphs.text: For most of human history, populations were shaped like pyramids: many children at the base, fewer adults above them and a narrow point of old people at the top. That shape was the product of high birth rates combined with high death rates at every age. In the course of the last two centuries, first in Europe and then almost everywhere, both rates have fallen, and the pyramid has been turning into something closer to a column. The change, known as demographic ageing, is one of the most predictable developments in the social sciences, since everyone who will be old in forty years’ time has already been born. Forecasts of the number of young people are far less certain, because they depend on births that have not yet happened.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Ageing has two causes, and they work on different timescales. The first is longer life. Life expectancy at birth has roughly doubled in many countries since the late nineteenth century, at first because far fewer children died young and later because adults began to survive illnesses of middle and old age. The second, and usually the more powerful, is falling fertility. When families have fewer children, each new generation is smaller than the one before, and the older generations make up a growing share of the whole population even if no one lives a day longer. Demographers often point out that a country could age quite rapidly without any improvement in health at all, simply because its birth rate had fallen.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The speed of the transition has varied enormously. In parts of western Europe, the share of the population aged over sixty-five took more than a century to double. In several East Asian countries, the same change has happened in little more than twenty years, because birth rates fell very quickly after the middle of the twentieth century. Speed matters as much as scale. A country that ages slowly has decades in which to adjust its pension system, its housing and its workforce, while one that ages quickly must make the same changes within a single political generation, often before the institutions that would manage them have fully developed.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The measure most often used to describe the economic consequences is the dependency ratio, which compares the number of people of working age with the number of children and older people. As a population ages, the ratio worsens, and governments worry that fewer workers will have to support more pensioners through taxes and contributions. Critics of the measure argue that it is misleading, because it assumes that everyone over a fixed age is dependent and everyone below it is working. In practice many people in their sixties continue to work, care for grandchildren or volunteer, while many younger adults are studying, unemployed or outside the labour market for other reasons, so that the ratio can overstate the burden considerably. Some economists therefore prefer measures based on how many people actually work, whatever their age.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Governments have responded in several ways. The most common has been to raise the age at which state pensions can be claimed, often linking it directly to life expectancy so that it rises automatically without a new decision each time. Others have tried to increase the share of adults in paid work, particularly among women and older workers, which can offset much of the effect of ageing on the dependency ratio. Immigration is also frequently proposed as a solution, but most demographic studies conclude that it can only slow the process, since immigrants themselves grow older and, over time, tend to have families of a similar size to those around them. None of these measures reverses ageing; they change only how its costs are shared.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Ageing also changes the shape of cities and regions. Young adults tend to move towards large cities for education and work, while older people are more likely to stay where they are or to move to smaller towns and coastal areas. Cities, as a result, often age more slowly than the countryside around them. In some rural districts the result has been a spiral of decline: as young people leave, schools and shops close, which in turn makes it harder to persuade young families to stay or to move in. Several countries now have villages in which most residents are over seventy and no child has been born for years, and local councils there face the unusual task of planning for a population that is certain to shrink.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: It is easy to describe all of this as a crisis, but many demographers resist the word, since it suggests an emergency that could have been avoided, when the causes are neither sudden nor unwelcome. An ageing population is, after all, largely the result of success: children who survive, adults who live long lives and parents who are able to choose how many children to have. The difficulty lies not in the fact of ageing but in institutions designed for a younger society, from pension systems created when retirement lasted only a few years to housing built for large families rather than for people living alone. Those institutions can be changed, however slowly; the age structure of the population, for the next half-century at least, largely cannot.
paragraphs.label: G

texts.title: The race that grew to forty-two kilometres

paragraphs.text: The marathon is the only major running event named after a story. According to a legend recorded several centuries after the events it describes, a messenger ran from the battlefield of Marathon to Athens to announce a Greek victory, delivered his message and died. Historians doubt almost every part of this account. The earliest historian of the war mentions a different runner, who covered a far longer distance to Sparta to ask for help, and says nothing about a death. But the legend was well known in the nineteenth century, and when the first modern Olympic Games were planned for Athens in 1896, a long road race from Marathon was proposed as a way of linking the new games with the ancient past. The race was a success, and its winner, a local water carrier, became a national hero.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The distance of that first race was about forty kilometres, a figure chosen because it was roughly the length of the road rather than for any historical reason. For the next few decades the length of a marathon was not fixed at all. Some courses were measured carefully; others were simply estimated from maps. Races were organised along whatever route was convenient between two places, and distances varied by several kilometres from one event to another. Runners and spectators do not seem to have minded. What mattered was the idea of a very long race that tested endurance rather than speed, and a record set on one course was not expected to be compared with a time achieved on another. A few races were even run on tracks, lap after lap, rather than on roads.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The now standard distance of 42.195 kilometres originated at the London Games of 1908. The organisers planned a course of about twenty-six miles from the grounds of a royal castle to the stadium, and adjustments to the start and the finish, including a decision to end the race in front of the royal box, added a little more. Whether the royal family actually asked for these changes is disputed, since the surviving records suggest that the organisers made the decisions themselves. The London distance was used again at several later races, and in 1921 the international athletics federation adopted it as the official length, so that times could at last be compared fairly. Many runners today regard the final 195 metres as the most painful part of the race.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The early marathons were dangerous in ways that modern ones are not. Runners were often given little water, because drinking during a race was widely believed to cause cramps, and some competitors took substances that were thought to improve stamina but in fact did the opposite. At several early Olympic marathons a large proportion of the starters failed to finish. In one early race the leader collapsed several times inside the stadium and was helped across the line, which led to his disqualification. Medical supervision of races became common only gradually, and the modern pattern of regular drinking stations along the course dates largely from the second half of the twentieth century, when research on athletes began to change what coaches advised.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: For most of its history the marathon was an event for a small number of trained athletes. That changed in the 1970s, when a boom in recreational running in North America and Europe led cities to open their marathons to anyone who wished to enter. Numbers grew rapidly: races that had attracted a few hundred runners soon drew tens of thousands, most of them with no hope of winning and no wish to. Organisers had to provide far more water, toilets and medical staff than ever before. For these runners the aim was simply to finish, or to beat their own previous time, and the marathon became as much a personal challenge and a public festival as a competition between athletes.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Women were among the last to be admitted. Well into the 1960s many officials believed that long-distance running was harmful to women, and they were barred from most official marathons. Some ran unofficially, starting from the roadside after the official start or entering under initials that concealed their sex. Officials who noticed sometimes tried to push them off the course. Pressure from runners and clubs gradually changed the rules, and a women’s marathon was included in the Olympic Games for the first time in 1984. Winning times in women’s races have since fallen far faster than those in men’s, which suggests how much talent had previously been excluded from the sport.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The large city marathons of today are also substantial economic events. They bring visitors who fill hotels and restaurants, and many have become major vehicles for charity fundraising, with runners collecting sponsorship for causes of their choice. Critics point out that closing a city’s roads for most of a day imposes costs on residents and businesses that do not benefit, and that entry fees have risen to levels that exclude many would-be runners. Even so, the demand for places far exceeds the supply in most large races, and several now allocate entries by lottery, so that even experienced runners cannot be sure of a place. Places are often reserved for runners who raise a set amount for charity.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: In many countries the local newspaper is disappearing, gradually in some places and suddenly in others. Titles that reported for a century or more on council meetings, court cases, school results and local sport have closed, merged or shrunk to a handful of staff covering a whole region. Researchers have begun to describe places with no dedicated local reporting at all as news deserts, and the number of such places has grown steadily over the past two decades. The obvious explanation is the internet, which took away the classified advertisements that once paid for most local journalism, but explaining the decline is easier than deciding whether anything can or should be done about it. Both questions matter, and they are too often confused.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: It is worth being clear about what is lost. Local papers were never mainly admired for their prose, and many of them were dull. Their value lay in routine attendance: a reporter who sat through every meeting of the planning committee, who read the council’s accounts and who knew which officials to ask. Much of what such reporters wrote was never read by more than a few hundred people, but its existence mattered. The political scientist Helen Marsh has found that when a local paper closes, fewer residents attend public meetings or respond to consultations, apparently because they know less about what their council is doing. Her research also suggests that the cost of borrowing for local authorities rises after a closure, since lenders regard councils that are less closely watched as a greater risk. Marsh is careful to say that her findings show an association and cannot prove that the closure alone is responsible.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Online sources have not filled the gap. Social media groups for a town or neighbourhood are often lively, but they mostly circulate opinion, complaints and rumour rather than verified information, and they rarely send anyone to sit through a three-hour committee meeting. National news organisations cover local stories only when they become dramatic enough to interest a national audience. The media researcher Daniel Frost describes the result as a two-tier system, in which large cities remain well reported while smaller towns receive attention only after something has already gone badly wrong. Frost adds that when national reporters do arrive, they rarely stay long enough to understand the background.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Several models have been tried to keep local reporting alive. Some newspapers have moved behind paywalls and ask readers to pay for online access, which has worked well for a few titles with loyal audiences but poorly for most. Others have become non-profit organisations supported by donations and grants from foundations, a model that has grown quickly in North America. The economist Ruth Adler, who has studied these non-profits, points out that they tend to be founded in wealthier areas where donors live, which means that the places most in need of reporting are the least likely to get it. Adler also notes that foundation grants are usually short, which makes it hard for a newsroom to plan beyond a year or two.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The most controversial proposal is public funding. In some countries governments already subsidise newspapers through reduced taxes or direct grants, and a few have created schemes that pay the salaries of reporters placed in local newsrooms. Critics argue that journalism paid for by the state cannot be trusted to hold the state to account. The worry is not only that governments might punish critical reporting but that editors might avoid it in order to keep their funding. I think this concern is real but manageable. Public broadcasting in many countries has shown that state funding can be combined with editorial independence, provided that the money is distributed by an independent body according to published rules rather than by ministers.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Another proposal is to make the large technology platforms pay for the news that appears on their services. Supporters argue that these platforms profit from the attention that journalism attracts while contributing little to its cost. Agreements of this kind have been introduced in a few countries and have brought significant sums to some publishers. Frost is sceptical, noting that most of the money has gone to large national organisations rather than to local titles, and that such deals make newspapers dependent on the goodwill of the very companies they are supposed to report on. The platforms, for their part, have sometimes responded by removing news from their services altogether.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: My own view is that no single model will be enough, and that the question should be framed differently. Local reporting is less like a product that people buy than like a public service, such as street lighting, which benefits everyone whether or not they pay for it, and nobody expects a street light to pay for itself. Seen in that way, the case for some combination of public money, charitable support and payment by readers becomes much easier to make. What matters in the end is not who pays but whether someone is still sitting in the committee room, taking notes, when the decisions that shape a town are made. That, in the end, is what a town loses when its newspaper closes.
paragraphs.label: G

Races were held to celebrate the victory.

explanation.en: The earliest historian mentions another runner who went much further, to Sparta → B. A is the legend; the historian mentions no death.
explanation.kk: Алғашқы тарихшы көмек сұрап Спартаға әлдеқайда алыс жүгірген басқа жүгірушіні атайды → B. A — аңыз, ал тарихшы өлім туралы ештеңе жазбайды.
explanation.ru: Ранний историк упоминает другого бегуна, который бежал гораздо дальше, в Спарту, за помощью → B. A — это легенда, а историк о смерти ничего не пишет.

items.quote: so that times could at last be compared fairly
items.prompt: What was one result of adopting a single official distance?

options.text: More women were allowed to enter races.
Courses had to finish in front of a royal box.
Races became shorter than before.
Times from different races could be compared.

explanation.en: “so that times could at last be compared fairly” → D.
explanation.kk: «so that times could at last be compared fairly» → D. 1921 жылға дейін қашықтық әртүрлі болған, рекордтарды салыстырмаған.
explanation.ru: «so that times could at last be compared fairly» → D. До 1921 года дистанции различались, и рекорды не сравнивали.

items.quote: a large proportion of the starters failed to finish
items.prompt: According to paragraph D, what happened at several early Olympic marathons?

options.text: Many runners did not complete the course.
Drinks were provided at regular points.
Runners were tested for banned substances.
Doctors followed the leading runners.

explanation.en: “a large proportion of the starters failed to finish” → A. Drinking stations (B) came much later.
explanation.kk: «a large proportion of the starters failed to finish» → A. Су беру пункттері (B) ХХ ғасырдың екінші жартысында ғана пайда болған.
explanation.ru: «a large proportion of the starters failed to finish» → A. Пункты питья (B) появились лишь во второй половине XX века.

items.quote: which suggests how much talent had previously been excluded from the sport
items.prompt: What does the writer suggest about the fall in women’s winning times?

options.text: Women’s courses have become easier.
Women now train harder than men do.
Many able runners had earlier been kept out.
Timing methods have improved since 1984.

explanation.en: “suggests how much talent had previously been excluded from the sport” → C.
explanation.kk: «suggests how much talent had previously been excluded from the sport» → C. Жаттығу (B) мен уақыт өлшеу (D) туралы мәтінде ештеңе жоқ.
explanation.ru: «suggests how much talent had previously been excluded from the sport» → C. О тренировках (B) и хронометраже (D) в тексте ничего нет.

groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

items.quote: Local papers were never mainly admired for their prose
items.prompt: Local newspapers were chiefly respected for the quality of their writing.

explanation.en: “Local papers were never mainly admired for their prose” → NO.
explanation.kk: «Local papers were never mainly admired for their prose» → NO: құндылығы тілшінің үнемі қатысуында болған.
explanation.ru: «Local papers were never mainly admired for their prose» → NO: ценность была в постоянном присутствии репортёра.

items.quote: Researchers have begun to describe places with no dedicated local reporting at all as news deserts
items.prompt: Areas without local reporting are more common in the countryside than in suburbs.

explanation.en: News deserts are growing in number, but countryside and suburbs are never compared → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.kk: Мұндай жерлер көбейіп жатқаны айтылған, бірақ ауылда көп пе, қала маңында көп пе — айтылмаған → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.ru: Сказано, что таких мест становится больше, но где их больше — в сёлах или пригородах, — не сказано → NOT GIVEN.

items.quote: Online sources have not filled the gap.
items.prompt: Neighbourhood groups on social media can take the place of a local reporter.

explanation.en: “Online sources have not filled the gap” → NO.
explanation.kk: «Online sources have not filled the gap»: топтар пікір мен өсек таратады, отырысқа бармайды → NO.
explanation.ru: «Online sources have not filled the gap»: группы распространяют мнения и слухи и не ходят на заседания → NO.

items.quote: which has worked well for a few titles with loyal audiences but poorly for most
items.prompt: Paywalls have worked better for newspapers in large cities than in small towns.

explanation.en: Paywalls helped only a few titles with loyal readers; city size is never mentioned → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.kk: Ақылы қолжетімділік адал оқырманы бар аз басылымға ғана көмектескені айтылған; қала көлеміне байланысы жоқ → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.ru: Сказано лишь, что платный доступ помог немногим изданиям с преданной аудиторией; связи с размером города нет → NOT GIVEN.

items.quote: provided that the money is distributed by an independent body according to published rules rather than by ministers
items.prompt: State money for journalism is acceptable if it is handed out by an independent organisation.

explanation.en: The writer finds the concern manageable “provided that the money is distributed by an independent body” → YES.
explanation.kk: Автор қауіпті «real but manageable» дейді, егер ақшаны тәуелсіз орган бөлсе → YES.
explanation.ru: Автор считает опасения «real but manageable» при условии, что деньги распределяет независимый орган → YES.

items.quote: have brought significant sums to some publishers
items.prompt: Payments from technology platforms have reduced the number of local newspapers closing.

explanation.en: Deals brought money to some, mainly large, publishers; their effect on closures is never stated → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.kk: Келісімдер кейбір баспагерлерге, көбіне ірілеріне, ақша әкелгені айтылған; жергілікті газеттердің жабылуына әсері айтылмаған → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.ru: Сказано, что соглашения принесли деньги некоторым издателям, в основном крупным; повлияли ли они на число закрытий местных газет, не сказано → NOT GIVEN.

groups.instruction: Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in Text 3? Write YES if the statement agrees with the claims of the writer, NO if the statement contradicts the claims of the writer, NOT GIVEN if it is impossible to say what the writer thinks about this.

items.quote: fewer residents attend public meetings or respond to consultations
items.prompt: Public involvement in local affairs falls after a newspaper closes.

explanation.en: Marsh: fewer residents attend meetings or respond to consultations → A.
explanation.kk: Marsh: газет жабылғаннан кейін жиналысқа баратын, пікір білдіретін тұрғын азаяды → A.
explanation.ru: Marsh: после закрытия газеты меньше жителей ходят на собрания и отвечают на консультации → A.

items.quote: smaller towns receive attention only after something has already gone badly wrong
items.prompt: Smaller communities are covered only once a serious problem has occurred.

explanation.en: Frost: smaller towns get attention only after something goes badly wrong → B.
explanation.kk: Frost: шағын қалаларға бір нәрсе бүлінгенде ғана назар аударылады → B.
explanation.ru: Frost: малые города получают внимание, только когда что-то уже пошло плохо → B.

items.quote: the places most in need of reporting are the least likely to get it
items.prompt: Charitable news organisations are least common where they are most needed.

explanation.en: Adler: non-profits appear where donors live, not where the need is greatest → C.
explanation.kk: Adler: коммерциялық емес редакциялар донорлар тұратын жерде ашылады, ең қажет жерде емес → C.
explanation.ru: Adler: некоммерческие редакции возникают там, где живут доноры, а не там, где нужнее всего → C.

items.quote: such deals make newspapers dependent on the goodwill of the very companies they are supposed to report on
items.prompt: Payments from technology companies may compromise the independence of newspapers.

explanation.en: Frost: such deals make papers dependent on the companies they report on → B. The writer discusses independence in E, but about state money.
explanation.kk: Frost: мұндай келісімдер газетті өзі жазуы тиіс компанияларға тәуелді етеді → B. Тәуелсіздік туралы автор да айтады (E абзацы), бірақ ол мемлекет ақшасына қатысты.
explanation.ru: Frost: такие сделки делают газеты зависимыми от компаний, о которых они должны писать → B. О независимости говорит и автор (абзац E), но там речь о государственных деньгах, а не о платформах.

options.text: Helen Marsh
Daniel Frost
Ruth Adler

groups.instruction: Look at the following statements and the list of people below. Match each statement with the correct person, A–C.

items.quote: the cost of borrowing for local authorities rises after a closure
items.prompt: What does Marsh’s research suggest about councils without a local paper?

options.text: They hold fewer public meetings.
Their accounts are published less often.
They pay more when they borrow money.
They employ more press officers.

explanation.en: “the cost of borrowing for local authorities rises after a closure” → C. A is a trap: fewer residents attend, not fewer meetings.
explanation.kk: «the cost of borrowing for local authorities rises after a closure» → C. A — тұзақ: жиналыс емес, оған келетін тұрғын азаяды.
explanation.ru: «the cost of borrowing for local authorities rises after a closure» → C. A — ловушка: меньше становится не собраний, а жителей на них.

items.quote: Local reporting is less like a product that people buy than like a public service, such as street lighting
items.prompt: What does the writer compare local reporting to?

options.text: A service like street lighting that benefits everyone
A product that readers choose to buy
A charity run by volunteers
A branch of public broadcasting

explanation.en: “less like a product that people buy than like a public service, such as street lighting” → A. B is what the writer rejects.
explanation.kk: «less like a product that people buy than like a public service, such as street lighting» → A. B — автор келіспейтін нәрсе.
explanation.ru: «less like a product that people buy than like a public service, such as street lighting» → A. B — как раз то, с чем автор не согласен.

items.quote: What matters in the end is not who pays but whether someone is still sitting in the committee room
items.prompt: What is the main point of the final paragraph?

options.text: Public money should replace all other funding.
Readers should be required to pay for local news.
Technology platforms should fund local reporting.
What counts is that reporting continues, whoever funds it.

explanation.en: “not who pays but whether someone is still sitting in the committee room” → D. A is a distractor: the writer wants a combination.
explanation.kk: «not who pays but whether someone is still sitting in the committee room» → D. A — алдамшы нұсқа: автор бірнеше көзді біріктіруді ұсынады.
explanation.ru: «not who pays but whether someone is still sitting in the committee room» → D. A — дистрактор: автор предлагает сочетание источников, а не одни государственные деньги.
